question: In its answer to my question E-000367/2025,1 the Commission acknowledged that unfair terms in foreign currency loans fall under Directive 93/13/EEC, but stated that it was not competent to intervene in the practices of Greek banks or the suspension of auctions.

However, in Greece, the incomplete transposition of Directive 2014/17/EU (in particular Article 11 on currency conversion, active conversion mechanism, specific information, consequences of infringement) and the concealment of unfair systemic practices constitute a breach of EU law.

Official banking data reveals that Greek banks, such as Piraeus Bank, granted massive loans in CHF without having the corresponding capital in CHF. The bank did not lend in francs but in euro, with leverage of up to 1:108. This practice constitutes structural opacity and deception, contrary to the judgments of the CJEU (C-186/16, C-520/21, C709/19). In view of the above: 1.

Will the Commission initiate infringement proceedings against Greece for the incomplete and incorrect transposition of Directive 2014/17/EU and for the failure to implement Directive 93/13/EEC on a systemic scale?
Will the Commission request from the European Banking Authority and the Bank of Greece official data on leverage, funding and compliance with transparency obligations in CHF loans?
Will the Commission consider issuing a recommendation to the Greek Government to suspend real estate auctions related to CHF loans temporarily until compliance with EU law is ensured?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2025) The Mortgage Credit Directive 2014/17/EU1, which applies to contracts concluded after 2016, provides a high level of consumer protection and specific rules on mortgage credits denominated in a foreign currency. The relevant rules regarding foreign currency loans (e.g.

the right to convert the credit agreement into an alternative currency) have been transposed by Greece in Article 12(1) (f) and Article 22 of L.4438/2016. The law has been assessed by the Commission and, based on the information available, there is no evidence of an incorrect or incomplete transposition.

Under the prudential framework, credit institutions are not obliged to comply with the liquidity2 3 and interest rate risk4 requirements in each currency in which they lend. Supervisors do monitor the liquidity and interest rate risk5 that might emerge from currency mismatches.

The Commission has received complaints concerning the implementation of Directives 2014/17/EU and 93/13/EEC in certain Member States, including Greece. The Commission is analysing them and will decide on possible next steps as appropriate.

It is the primary responsibility of the national authorities and courts to ensure the monitoring and enforcement of the application of consumer law in individual business-to-consumer relationships, considering the circumstances of each case, and to provide redress where appropriate6.
